title.full: Global energy and climate outlook 2024 – Updating NDCs and closing the ambition gap – Indicators for 1.5°C alignment

description: Global normative pathway peaking at 1.5°C warming before declining to 1.3°C by 2100.

coreDrivers.policies: The scenario implements current and legislated policies as of July 2024, as in Reference scenario. An additional high-ambition global uniform carbon price starts in 2025 and rises over time.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Global pathway is constrained to limit warming to 1.5°C by 2100 with net zero around 2060 and negative emissions later.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Technology learning are endogenously developed in POLES-JRC; cost trend decreases as much as the technology is being adopted.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Annual power-sector investment doubles between 2020 and 2050, peaking in 2040. Solar and wind continue to dominate the technology mix, while storage becomes material from 2035 onward. Unabated fossil-fuel investment is no longer material by 2040, whereas CCS investment peaks in 2030 and remains material through 2050. Those investments increase GCP by 0.1% compared to reference scenario. As GDP also doubles over the same period, power-sector investment remains broadly constant as a share of GDP.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP assumptions are shared across the GECO scenarios and set the activity baseline. Inputs combine World Bank, IMF, OECD/SSP2, EU Ageing Report and JRC-IIASA sources.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: The models assumed limited explicit behavioural-change modelling compared to Reference scenario. Household, transport and housing expenditure shifts are reported as macro effects.

dependencies.dependency_description: The pathway adds an uniform global carbon price to the July 2024 legislated policy setup.

Quantitative fuel-price, investment and constraint emissions budget show that least-cost competition and technology costs strongly shape the power transition. However, the carbon-price values are not published.
The models assumed limited explicit behavioural-change modelling compared to Reference scenario. Household, transport and housing expenditure shifts are reported as macro effects.
Very high wind and solar deployment and storage investment indicate grid and flexibility requirements, but indicators availability on transmission and distribution remains low.

Power-sector delivery depends on storage becoming cheaper and scaling sufficiently, and on CCS being deployable for residual fossil and biomass generation. Those two conditions are bidning constraints to respect 1.5°C carbon budget.

Wind, solar and other renewables are associated with potentials and supply curves per country. This scenario is the most ambitous using POLES-JRC and this is where renewables availability will be the main constraint.

Moderate: renewable-power employment rises from 1.9 million jobs in 2020 to 11.9 million in 2035 and 17.2 million in 2050, implying substantial workforce scaling and reallocation; GECO does not identify specific shortages.
The pathway adds an uniform global carbon price to the July 2024 legislated policy setup.
"Moderate: inferred from carbon-price design and fuel switching; Higher fuel costs/carbon prices likely affect aviation demand/fuel choice, but no passenger/freight economics are provided.".
The pathway models an increase in public transportation (including air travel) until 2040 compared to Reference scenario, then a decrease in mobility in 2050.

The scenario requires some large sustainable aviation fuel and e-fuel capacity construction. This relies on some infracture needs. Production and distribution infrastructure are not tabulated by airport/route.

To limit emissions in the aviation sector, 1.5°C scenario is reliant on sustauniable aviation fuel expansion. Hydrogen and electricity aircraft are also deployed in the scenario by 2035. H2 and e-fuels represents 42% in sectoral energy demand.
The pathway adds an uniform global carbon price to the July 2024 legislated policy setup.
GECO states that green-hydrogen costs remain high and provides quantitative steel emissions, CCS and biomass shares showing the resulting preference for other abatement routes.
Carbon Capture and Storage is a new technology which 1.5°C is reliant to decarbonize steel sector. This requires some infrastructure, but those are not detailed in the pathway.

To respect 1.5°C carbon budget, steel decarbonisation depends materially on industrial CCS becoming deployable at scale, while hydrogen-based primary steel remains an emerging option. 37% of Steel emissions are captured with CCS in 2050/.
Moderate: scrap availability and quality requirements constrain EAF recycling.
